prompt: A new office building on a corporate campus is served by its own surface parking lot and stormwater pond. To lower the reported impervious area, the owner asks the team to draw the LEED boundary around the building footprint and entry plaza alone. How should the LEED AP respond?

Accept it, provided the parking lot is certified later as a separate LEED project
Reject it, since facilities serving normal operations belong in the boundary
Reject it, since the LEED boundary has to match the legal property line exactly

explanation: The minimum program requirement for reasonable LEED boundaries says the boundary must include the land and facilities that support the building's normal operations, such as its parking, bicycle storage, and stormwater features. Drawing the line tightly around the footprint to hide impervious parking is gerrymandering, which the MPR prohibits even though the boundary may legitimately be smaller than the owned parcel.

distractorExplanations.a: Boundary choice is constrained by the MPRs; the team cannot exclude features that serve the building just to improve credit results.
distractorExplanations.b: Certifying the lot separately does not fix the problem, because a facility serving this building's daily operation belongs inside this project's boundary.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the LEED boundary with the property boundary; on a campus the LEED boundary can be smaller than the legal parcel as long as it is reasonable.

prompt: A 100,000 sq ft mixed-use building has 55,000 sq ft of apartments and 45,000 sq ft of ground-floor retail and offices. How does the LEED 40/60 rule guide rating system selection?

Certify the residential and commercial portions as two separate projects

Choose the more appropriate rating system, since neither use exceeds 60%

explanation: Under the 40/60 rule, a rating system should not be used if it fits less than 40% of the floor area, should be used if it fits more than 60%, and is the team's choice when the share falls between 40% and 60%. prompt: An office has 40 staff working 8-hour days and 20 part-time staff working 4 hours per day. What full-time equivalent (FTE) occupancy should the team use?

options.text: 40 FTE
50 FTE
60 FTE
80 FTE

explanation: FTE normalizes occupants to an 8-hour workday: each person's daily hours are divided by 8. The 40 full-time staff count as 40 FTE and the 20 part-timers at 4 hours each count as 0.5 FTE apiece, adding 10 FTE, for 50 FTE. This figure then feeds occupant-based calculations such as fixture water use and long-term bicycle storage.

distractorExplanations.a: Counts the full-time staff but drops the part-time workers, who still contribute 10 FTE based on their 4-hour days.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats every part-time worker as a full FTE, overstating occupancy by ignoring that each works half of an 8-hour day.
distractorExplanations.d: Doubles the part-time contribution instead of halving it, which inflates the occupancy used in water and bicycle calculations.

prompt: In a law office, conversations in an enclosed meeting room are clearly understood in the adjacent private office, even though the shared wall uses a well-rated partition assembly. The wall stops at the suspended ceiling. What is the most effective correction?

Installing sound masking in the open office outside both rooms
Adding a second gypsum layer to the existing partition face
Extending the partition to the deck and sealing penetrations

prompt: A lighting designer is comparing two troffer options for a large open-plan office where staff work at screens all day. Which metric should guide the choice to limit discomfort glare from the luminaires themselves?

prompt: The owner of a combined retail and photo studio space asks how to judge whether new LED fixtures will show fabrics and skin tones accurately. Which metrics describe that property?

Color Rendering Index or the TM-30 fidelity index
Correlated color temperature listed in kelvin units
Light reflectance values of the walls and ceilings

distractorExplanations.d: Surface reflectance measures how much light walls and ceilings return, which shapes brightness distribution, not the color quality of the source.

prompt: A daylight simulation for a south-facing open office shows strong spatial daylight autonomy (sDA) results but also a large floor area exceeding the annual sunlight exposure (ASE) criterion. What does this combination tell the team, and what is the right response?

options.text: Daylight is insufficient deep in the plan, so add skylights to lift sDA further
The model is invalid, because high sDA and high ASE cannot occur together
Daylight is ample but direct sun risks glare, so add shading or redirection
Perimeter fixtures can be deleted, since sDA shows daylight covers all hours

explanation: sDA measures daylight sufficiency: the share of floor area reaching a target illuminance from daylight for at least half of annual occupied hours. ASE measures excess: the share of area receiving high direct-sun illuminance for many hours a year, a proxy for glare and overheating. High sDA with high ASE means plenty of light but uncontrolled sun, so the team adds exterior shading, light shelves or light-redirecting glazing and reruns the model.

distractorExplanations.a: Low sDA would signal insufficient daylight; here sDA is already strong, and more skylights would add direct sun and worsen the ASE result.
distractorExplanations.b: The two metrics measure different things and commonly both run high on unshaded south glazing; that exact pattern is why ASE is paired with sDA.
distractorExplanations.d: sDA counts only part of the occupied hours, so cloudy days and dark hours still need electric light, ideally with daylight-responsive controls.

prompt: The permanent air handlers on a BD+C project must run during interior finishing to temper and dry the building. What should the construction IAQ management plan require for the air system?

Rely on the factory filters and clean the coils at final turnover
Seal supply diffusers while leaving return openings unfiltered

explanation: If permanently installed HVAC operates during construction, SMACNA's HVAC protection measure applies: install filtration media at return grilles and openings, seal duct openings not in use, and replace all filtration media immediately before occupancy. prompt: A project beside a busy port has poor outdoor air quality and a high cooling load. The engineer proposes designing ventilation with the ASHRAE 62.1 Indoor Air Quality Procedure (IAQP) instead of the Ventilation Rate Procedure. What does the IAQP require that the prescriptive method does not?

Applying tabulated per-person and per-area outdoor air rates to every zone, then correcting for air distribution effectiveness and system efficiency
Placing operable windows within a set distance of each occupant and keeping those openings free of permanent obstructions
Supplying 100 percent outdoor air with energy recovery so that no recirculated air reaches any occupied zone

explanation: The Ventilation Rate Procedure is prescriptive: tabulated outdoor air rates per person and per area. The IAQP is performance-based: the designer identifies contaminants and their sources, sets target concentrations and perceived air quality criteria, and uses mass-balance analysis (and/or subjective evaluation) to show that outdoor air combined with air cleaning meets the targets. That lets a project with poor outdoor air lean on filtration and gas-phase cleaning.

distractorExplanations.b: That describes the Ventilation Rate Procedure itself, the prescriptive method the engineer is proposing to move away from.
distractorExplanations.c: That is the 62.1 natural ventilation procedure, a separate path built on operable openings rather than contaminant targets.
distractorExplanations.d: 100 percent outdoor air is a system choice, not an IAQP requirement; the IAQP usually aims to reduce outdoor air by adding air cleaning.

prompt: A BD+C project is located in a region that does not meet national ambient air quality standards for fine particulates, and the building will be mechanically ventilated. Which design response best addresses local outdoor air quality?

Filtering outdoor air and siting intakes away from local sources
Raising the outdoor air rate so indoor particulates are diluted more quickly
CO2 demand control so the outdoor air rate drops whenever particulates rise

explanation: ASHRAE 62.1 asks designers to investigate regional and local outdoor air quality. Where the area is in nonattainment for particulates, outdoor air must be filtered before it reaches occupied spaces, and intakes must be separated from local sources such as roads, loading docks and exhausts. Filtration plus careful intake placement treats the outdoor air the building still has to bring in.

distractorExplanations.c: When outdoor air is itself the particulate source, more unfiltered outdoor air raises indoor PM levels instead of diluting them.
